statement.p: The following questions refer to the table shown below, giving the temperature adjusted for wind-chill, C, in {}^\circ F, as a function f(w,T) of the wind speed, w, in mph, and the temperature, T, in {}^\circ F. The temperature adjusted for wind-chill tells you how cold it feels, as a result of the combination of wind and temperature.

p.em: Be sure you can state in practical terms what your answer means.
Be sure you can state in practical terms what your answer means.

static.solution:
(a) For f_w(10, 15) we know f_w(w_0, t_0) \approx \frac{f(w_0 + h,t_0) - f(w_0,t_0)}{h}.
Thus, we have f_w(10, 15) \approx \frac{0 - 3}{5} = -0.6.
Note that we could also approximate the partial derivative by taking a difference quotient with the point to the left of 10 (that is, taking f_w(10,15)\approx \frac{f(10,15) - f(10-5),15}{5}, or by taking a central difference, f_w(10,15)\approx \frac{f(10+5,15) - f(10-5,15)}{10}.
This means that when the wind speed is 10 mph and the true temperature is 15 {}^\circ F, as the wind speed increases from 10 mph by 1 mph we feel an approximately -0.6^\circ F drop in temperature. This rate is negative because the temperature you feel drops as the wind speed increases.
(b) For f_t(20, 25) we know f_t(w_0, t_0) \approx \frac{f(w_0,t_0 + h) - f(w_0,t_0)}{h}.
Thus, we have f_t(20, 25) \approx \frac{(17 - 11)}{5} = 1.2.
Note that we could also approximate the partial derivative by taking a difference quotient with the point to the left of 25 (that is, taking f_t(20,25)\approx \frac{f(20,25) - f(20,25-5)}{5}, or by taking a central difference, f_t(20,25)\approx \frac{f(20,25+5) - f(20,25-5)}{10}.
This means that when the wind speed is 20 mph and the true temperature is 25 {}^\circ F, the apparent temperature increases by approximately 1.2^\circ F for an increase of 1^\circ F in the true temperature. This rate is positive because the temperature you feel increases as the true temperature increases.
